A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same token-pricing study and provide readable main text, Figures 1–12, Table 1, and Appendices A–C. Content can be reliably matched despite repagination and editorial changes.

before.justification: v2 reports original experiments on tokenization misreporting, provider utility, GPU energy consumption, and multilingual pricing using LMSYS prompts and Llama, Gemma, and Ministral models.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and their results in the main text and Appendix C, including energy measurements and language-stratified profit margins.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1 and 2 retain the same splitting procedures and plausibility checks. The pay-per-character mechanism and its price-calibration prescription also remain unchanged. Distinguishing the random and heuristic policies with superscripts R and H changes notation, not procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use LMSYS-Chat-1M prompts for the same tokenization and pricing tasks, retaining English, Spanish, Russian, and Chinese coverage. The new competition example in Section 3.1 is analytical, not an evaluated test scenario.

E2.justification: Matched experiments retain the same reference comparisons, including truthful reporting for utility gains and pay-per-token pricing for the pricing transition. Newly discussed related works are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix A and the figure/table captions retain the same prompt filtering, sample sizes, model configurations, temperature and top-p settings, multilingual calibration/evaluation procedure, and energy-measurement protocols.

E4.justification: Appendix C retains the same model/temperature sensitivity analyses, tokenization examples, generation-versus-verification energy analysis, and language-stratified margins. The new market and legal discussion does not introduce an empirical robustness test or case study.

E5.justification: Both versions report five independent generations with different seeds and symmetric 90% confidence intervals using the stated t-distribution value of 2.015. Repeated-run and uncertainty-reporting practices in the captions also match.

E6.justification: The plotted results, Table 1 values, and experimental findings are unchanged. For example, Section 3.3 retains Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct overcharging maxima of 11.2%, 1.8%, and 0.28% for p = 0.99, 0.95, and 0.90, respectively. Appendix results and tokenization examples also match.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 adds a short competition calculation: reducing token price by a factor alpha while inflating reported length by approximately 1/alpha preserves per-output revenue. It explicitly assumes users break utility ties in favor of lower advertised token prices. Existing theorems, definitions, and Appendix B proofs remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The five enumerated contributions and substantive abstract/conclusion claims are retained. However, v3 removes the introduction's explicit claim to be the first work exploring incentive-compatible token pricing, adopting complementary positioning relative to prior pricing research instead.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands the interpretation of the threat through a competitive-entry argument and a new legal, reputational, and regulatory discussion explaining why these safeguards may not prevent misreporting. It also expresses stronger confidence in generalization to untested proprietary models and removes v2's explicit misuse-risk paragraph. The principal-agent role qualification is relocated to Section 2, rather than newly introduced.

D1.justification: Appendix A retains the same hardware descriptions, software libraries, generation settings, system prompt, energy-recording instructions, model/data links, and licensing information. The experimental code-access statement is also unchanged; citation and footnote renumbering do not alter reproducibility information.

R1.justification: Section 1.2 substantially revises research positioning, adding literature on alternative tokenizers, information and digital-service pricing, and data/model marketplaces. The closest-work discussion shifts from Sun et al. to Saig et al., emphasizing complementary strategic behaviors. Section 5 adds credible-auction and credence-goods references, while several earlier citations, including the adversarial-attack group, are removed.

P1.justification: v3 edits the abstract, introduces numbered Contributions and Related Work subsections, restructures related-work paragraphs, moves the principal-agent qualification earlier, distinguishes policy notation, and updates affiliations. The Damascus illustration changes from eight reported tokens to four. These edits are localized; the technical narrative, section order, and appendices largely retain their wording.

P2.justification: All figures, tables, and algorithms are retained. Reflow changes their placement, including some appendix displays. Table 1 abbreviates its generation/verification column headings and adjusts column spacing; the bibliography changes from numbered to author-year formatting. The plotted data and panel structures remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 improves clarity through distinct policy notation, earlier explanation of the principal-agent qualification, and a more precise comparison with prior auditing and pricing research. These provide a limited overall benefit without changing the experimental evidence or existing proofs. The removal of the explicit misuse discussion and stronger confidence about untested proprietary models weaken the caveats and temper the improvement.
